title: Give a new name a second use.
kicker: Remember names by using them naturally

source.title: How to Win Friends and Influence People · Remember names

steps.label: The moment you miss it
steps.text: Introductions often happen while you are thinking about what to say next. Carnegie treats remembering someone’s name as a small way of recognizing them as a person.

steps.label: Use it once
steps.text: If someone introduces themselves as Morgan, answer naturally: ‘Good to meet you, Morgan.’ If you missed the pronunciation, ask them to say it again. Then listen for a detail that connects the name to the conversation.

steps.label: Practice the recall
steps.text: Before you meet again, see if you can retrieve the name and the detail. A single natural use and a later recall attempt give you two chances to pay attention.

question: What can you do immediately after hearing someone’s name to help remember it?
answer: Use it naturally once and connect it to a detail you heard from them.
takeaway: Use the name once, connect it to a real detail, and recall it later.

title: Write the finish line before you start.
kicker: Begin with the end in mind

source.title: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People · Habit 2

steps.label: The open task
steps.text: ‘Make a training guide’ can mean a two-page reference or a forty-page manual. Covey’s second habit asks you to picture the desired result before deciding how to get there.

steps.label: An observable result
steps.text: ‘A new technician can run the three checks without calling me’ gives the guide a test. It tells you what to include and when another page is adding work instead of clarity.

steps.label: Try it
steps.text: Before your next project, write one sentence that describes what a successful result lets someone do. Ask the person who needs the work whether that matches what they had in mind.

question: What makes a useful finish line for a project?
answer: An observable result that you and the people who need the work can recognize.
takeaway: Name what someone can do when the work is finished.

title: Pick your go signal before the pressure hits.

source.title: The Art of War · Tactical Dispositions, section 15
source.byline: Sun Tzu · translated by Lionel Giles

steps.label: Prepare before commitment
steps.text: Sun Tzu puts preparation ahead of committing to battle. A practical application is to decide what must be true before you take an expensive or hard-to-reverse step.

steps.label: A workable signal
steps.text: You are considering a change to a shared lab. Pick a go signal in advance: the test works on a spare setup, and a teammate has walked through the rollback with you.

steps.label: Use the signal
steps.text: If a deadline approaches and the check is still missing, you can explain exactly what remains. The signal gives you a way to discuss readiness when everyone feels pressure to move.

question: Why pick a go signal before you are under pressure?
answer: It gives you an observable readiness test when urgency might otherwise drive the decision.
takeaway: Decide which concrete checks make you ready before committing.
